title: Ukodo
localName: Ukodo — epuru, yam and pepper soup pottage
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: Two kilos of goat and four to five litres of water with a pepper-soup spice mix in exact proportions — and a piece of the cooked yam mashed back in as the thickener.
longDesc: Ukodo is New Year's Day food among the Urhobo, a one-pot of goat, yam and pepper-soup spice eaten for breakfast or brunch. Two things make it worth having. The spice mix is given in exact proportions — eight urheri to four erhe to two gbafilo to two umilo — which is the most precise pepper-soup specification in the whole record. And the thickening move is specific to this dish: once the yam is cooked you take it out, mash or blend one piece back into the broth to bring it to a consistency between yogurt and liquid milk, and return the rest just before serving.
ingredients: 2 kg goat meat, preferably the more fragrant he-goat, cut into bite-sized pieces
2-3 heaped tbsp pepper soup spice mix — see below
4-5 lemon grass leaves, bruised and tied into a bundle
Native salt, about 1/2 tsp or to taste
2 tbsp dry pepper (red chilli flakes), or to taste
Fresh yellow chilies, split in half, to be fished out once cooked
Nigerian yam, peeled and cut into chunks about 8 cm lengthways
// Pepper soup spice mix — proportions, not weights
8 skins or barks of urheri (grains of Selim)
// Used in the method but not listed in the original
Palm oil, to top before serving
equipment: Very large pot with a lid
steps: Put the goat meat, water, pepper soup spice mix, lemon grass, salt, dry pepper, yellow chilies if using, and ground crayfish into a large pot.
Bring to the boil, then turn down to simmer 30 to 40 minutes with the lid on, until the meat is halfway cooked.
Add a bit more water and check the seasoning. The pepper soup spice flavour should come through distinctly, with consistent heat from the chilli flakes.
Add the chunks of yam and cook until soft — a knife or fork inserted into a piece should slide in with ease.
Once the yams are cooked, remove them. Fish out the lemon grass leaves and discard them.
Thicken the soup to a consistency between yogurt and liquid milk by mashing or blending a piece of the yam back in.
Check the seasoning — salt, chilli — and adjust, then add the lime leaves if using.
Turn off the heat and set aside.
When ready to serve, put the yam back in and heat through until the soup and the yam are hot.
Top with palm oil before serving.
chefTips: The spice proportions are 8 : 4 : 2 : 2 — urheri, erhe, gbafilo, umilo. That is the most precise pepper-soup spice specification in any source consulted and it is worth making a batch of.
Take the yam out once it is cooked. Left in, it absorbs the liquid and disintegrates, and you lose both the broth and the chunks.
One piece of yam mashed back in is the thickener. Between yogurt and liquid milk is the target.
He-goat is specified for being more fragrant. It is also tougher, which is what the thirty-to-forty-minute first simmer is for.
Bruise the lemongrass by rubbing it between your palms and tie it in a bundle so you can pull it out whole.
Knife or fork sliding in with ease is the yam cue. Ukodo yam should be soft but still a chunk.
The palm oil goes on at the very end, over the top, and it is not in the original ingredient list. A cooking spoon is about right.
commonMistakes: Leaving the yam in the pot while the soup finishes.
Skipping the mash-back and serving it thin.
Losing the lemongrass in the pot because it was not tied.
Adding the palm oil early, where it muddies the clear pepper-soup broth.
sources: Adapted from 'Ukodo – Nigerian Yam & Pepper Soup Pottage for New Year's Day', published on kitchenbutterfly.com. ATTRIBUTION: byline prints as 'By Kitchen Butterfly', the site name, not 'Ozoz Sokoh'; credited to the site. Published Jan 3, 2014, Modified June 3, 2026, the latter part of a site-wide bulk stamp.

THE HEADNOTE, verbatim, and the best occasion-and-ethnicity note in the region: 'Ukodo is typical New Year's day fare for breakfast/brunch dish eaten by the Urhobos in the south of Nigeria (The Itsekiris, also of the Niger Delta call their version Epuru).' That parenthesis is the only source consulted that gives the Itsekiri name.

Quantities as printed: 2 kg goat meat, preferably the more fragrant he-goat; 4–5 litres of water; 2–3 heaped tablespoons of pepper soup spice mix; 4–5 lemon grass leaves, bruised by rubbing between your palms and tied into a bundle; native salt, about 1/2 a teaspoon or to taste; 2 tablespoon dry pepper (red chilli flakes) or to taste; fresh yellow chilies, split in half (to be fished out once cooked); Nigerian yam, peeled and cut into chunks, about 8cm lengthways; 2 teaspoons of ground crayfish (optional); '1/2 young lime leaves (optional)'.

THE SPICE MIX, given as proportions rather than weights: 8 skins/barks of Urheri (Grains of Selim); 4 seeds of Erhe (Calabash Nutmeg); 2 seeds of Gbafilo; 2 seeds of Umilo. This 8:4:2:2 specification is the most precise pepper-soup spice breakdown found anywhere — every other source either uses a commercial blend or gives no breakdown.

QUANTITY GAPS flagged: the YAM ITSELF, the central ingredient, has NO quantity — only a cut dimension, 'about 8cm lengthways'. The fresh yellow chilies carry no quantity. And '1/2 young lime leaves' is printed exactly thus and is ambiguous; it is given above without the fraction rather than guessed at.
LIST/METHOD MISMATCH, flagged: palm oil appears in method step 10 — 'Top with palm oil before serving' — but is NOT in the ingredient list. It is listed above under a clear heading.

Times and cues as printed: simmer 30 to 40 minutes with the lid on 'till the meat is halfway cooked'; the yam is done when 'a knife or fork inserted into a piece should slide in with ease'; thicken 'to the desired consistency by mashing or blending a piece of yam'. Yield is NOT specified despite 2 kg of goat and 4 to 5 litres of water, so the serving figure here is a serving suggestion.

A FURTHER GAP: plantain is mentioned in the page's own description of ukodo as a pottage of meat, vegetables, yams and plantains, but plantain does NOT appear in the ingredient list or anywhere in the method. That omission is in the source.
The page also makes a point worth keeping: Nigerian cuisine extends beyond heat, encompassing complex multi-layered spice blends combining floral, woody and nutty notes.

LEAD NOT RETRIEVED: the same site's 'On Pepper Soup Spice & Finding Names' (2018) is, by its title, likely the fullest treatment anywhere of the urheri, erhe, gbafilo and umilo names. It was not retrieved and remains the highest-value outstanding item for this entry.
storage: 4 days refrigerated. Keep the yam chunks in the broth.
reheating: Gentle heat until the yam is hot through.
healthBenefits: Goat is leaner than beef or lamb and lower in saturated fat.
Grains of Selim and calabash nutmeg are traditionally used as digestives.
Yam supplies potassium and resistant starch.
No added fat until the palm oil at the end.
culturalNote: Ukodo is a New Year's Day dish and that fixes it in the calendar in a way few Nigerian foods are. The Itsekiri call their version epuru. It is breakfast or brunch rather than dinner, it is eaten hot in a pepper-soup broth strong enough to clear the head, and the goat is specified as he-goat because the stronger smell is wanted rather than avoided.
